title: Multi-Entity Accounting Software: What Works at Each Stage
summary: Multi entity accounting software compared by stage: QuickBooks Online workarounds, Xero, Sage Intacct, and NetSuite, with the decision criteria that matter.
body_text: What Multi-Entity Accounting Software Does True multi entity accounting software does four things single-entity tools can’t do cleanly. Accounting software for multiple entities has to keep a separate ledger per legal entity, automate the transactions that flow between them, run the eliminations that keep internal activity out of group results, and consolidate on demand. Separate ledgers, one login. A distinct general ledger for each legal entity, ideally under one shared chart of accounts. Intercompany automation. Matched due-to and due-from entries when one entity bills, funds, or allocates cost to another. Automated eliminations. Intercompany revenue, expense, receivables, and payables never inflate the consolidated numbers. Consolidation. Each entity translates into one reporting currency and rolls up into a single group statement. The backbone standard here is FASB ASC 810, Consolidation. Under U.S. GAAP, a parent that holds a controlling financial interest presents the group as a single economic entity, and all intercompany balances and transactions are eliminated in full. That includes intercompany sales, loans, dividends, management fees, and open account balances. FASB’s Accounting Standards Update 2015-02 sets out the voting-interest and variable-interest-entity control models. The distinction that trips up buyers is elimination automation versus reporting. A management-reporting tool can net out intercompany lines for a board deck. A true multi entity accounting system posts the elimination as a journal entry, on the books, with an audit trail. Netted in a report isn’t eliminated on the ledger. That gap is exactly what separates the stages below. QuickBooks Online Workarounds for Early Multi-Entity QuickBooks Online has no native multi-entity consolidation. Each legal entity needs its own subscription, its own chart of accounts, and its own login, and nothing inside the platform combines them. That’s a documented product boundary, not a setup mistake. For a company running two or three domestic entities, the workarounds are real and hold for a while. Separate files plus class and location tracking. The common early pattern is one QBO company file per entity, then class and location tracking to segment activity inside a file. That tracking exists only on QuickBooks Online Plus and Advanced , and on Plus the cap is 40 combined classes and locations. It gives you segmentation inside one entity, not a substitute for separate legal-entity ledgers. Consolidation add-ons. Because QBO won’t consolidate, teams bolt on a reporting layer. Tools like Fathom pull each file into a group report and can consolidate hundreds of entities with account-level eliminations. The catch, stated by the vendors themselves, is that these produce management reports, not audit-ready consolidated statements. Where it breaks. Intercompany entries are manual, eliminations are hand-built in Excel every period, and QuickBooks carries a name-list ceiling around 100,000 records per file. When the close runs two weeks, the workaround has become the job. Working inside QuickBooks with a finance partner isn’t an either-or, as our take on QuickBooks versus a managed finance team lays out, and you can size up the feature limits of each QuickBooks tier before you commit. Intuit’s newer Intuit Enterprise Suite is positioned as the native step above separate QBO files, but for most growth-stage groups the practical next move is a mid-market ledger. Mid-Market Options: Xero and Sage Intacct The mid-market splits into two different answers. One is a small-stack alternative to QuickBooks. The other is a native multi-entity ledger. Xero: the small-stack alternative Xero handles a single entity’s multi-currency reasonably well, but like QuickBooks it has no native cross-organization consolidation. Each legal entity is a separate Xero organization with its own subscription and database. Consolidating multiple organizations has been one of the most-requested items on Xero’s own product-ideas forum for years, with a posted status of “not currently planned.” Multi-entity Xero users therefore rely on the same class of add-on as QBO for group reporting. Xero is a legitimate small-business ledger, but on the multi-entity question it lands where QuickBooks does. Entity-level books plus a bolt-on reporting layer, not a consolidation engine. Sage Intacct: the mid-market native Sage Intacct is where multi-entity stops being a workaround. It runs multiple legal entities inside one shared environment, with a common chart of accounts and a dimensional structure (entity, department, location, project, customer, vendor) instead of a pile of separate files. It generates due-to and due-from entries automatically, and its Advanced Consolidations module runs rule-based eliminations and daily-rate currency translation , and handles minority interest. Sage cites up to a 79% reduction in close time from these automations. Adoption is strongest in nonprofit, SaaS accounting , healthcare, and professional services, with a commonly cited fit around $5M to $200M revenue running two or more entities. For finance teams weighing the best software for multi-entity consolidation without a full ERP, Sage Intacct is the mid-market default. Pricing signals the tier change. Xero runs roughly $25 to $90 per organization per month. Sage Intacct is quote-only, with third-party estimates from ERP Research putting full users near $400 to $800 per user per month and typical annual spend from about $15,000 into six figures once consolidation and revenue-recognition modules are added. G2’s accounting category and TechnologyAdvice’s multi-entity roundup both track Sage Intacct as a leading finance-led choice. When NetSuite Becomes the Answer NetSuite OneWorld becomes the answer when the group goes global or when accounting is one module of a broader ERP need. OneWorld is the multi-subsidiary edition of Oracle NetSuite. It runs multiple legal entities in a single account, with each subsidiary keeping its own base currency, tax rules, and books, while corporate finance gets real-time consolidation without manual uploads. The scale figures are the reason to reach for it. OneWorld supports up to 250 subsidiaries per account , more than 190 currencies, 27 languages, and automated tax compliance in over 100 countries through its SuiteTax engine. It posts each transaction at both the local and headquarters level automatically, maps it to the parent in the correct currency at the appropriate exchange rate, and runs eliminations and consolidation at local, regional, and global roll-up levels. The practical dividing line versus Sage Intacct is scope. Choose NetSuite OneWorld when the requirement includes many foreign subsidiaries, native multi-currency consolidation across a deep hierarchy, country-specific tax engines, and a single system that also runs inventory, order management, or supply chain. Choose a finance-first native like Sage Intacct when the need is accounting depth and consolidation without a full ERP footprint. Scope, not headcount, makes the call. NetSuite pricing reflects the wider scope, with third-party estimates putting it roughly in the $25,000 to $100,000-plus per year range depending on modules and users, generally above Sage Intacct at equivalent scale. Readers who want the platform-versus-platform view can work through our NetSuite versus QuickBooks head-to-head , which drills into the two-system comparison this roundup deliberately keeps at arm’s length. Decision Criteria by Stage Six variables drive the selection, not brand preference. Whether you call it a multi entity accounting system or multi company accounting software, entity count, foreign subsidiaries, transaction volume, audit horizon, budget, and in-house admin capacity together point to a tier. Criterion Early stage (2-3 entities) Mid-market (native multi-entity) Global scale Typical fit QuickBooks Online (or Xero) + consolidation add-on Sage Intacct NetSuite OneWorld Entity count 2-3 domestic entities ~3-25 entities Deep hierarchy, up to 250 subsidiaries Foreign subsidiaries None or one, minimal FX Some, daily-rate translation needed Many, 190+ currencies, per-sub base currency Transaction volume Low to moderate Moderate to high High, plus inventory and supply chain Audit horizon No near-term audit Audit likely within 1-2 years Audit and multi-jurisdiction statutory filings Intercompany + eliminations Manual, in spreadsheets Automated due-to/due-from + rule-based eliminations Automated at local/regional/global roll-up Budget (indicative) ~$25-$99/mo per entity + add-on ~$15k into six figures/yr, quote-based ~$25k-$100k+/yr, quote-based In-house admin capacity Owner or one bookkeeper Controller-led finance team Finance team + ERP admin Two rules cut through it. The first trigger for leaving QuickBooks or Xero isn’t revenue. It’s the moment manual eliminations become the bottleneck of the close, commonly around the $10M to $20M mark or when the close crosses two weeks. The second is the foreign-subsidiary test. Once you have to translate foreign entities at daily rates and file locally in multiple countries, a native multi-currency consolidation engine stops being optional. G2 and TechnologyAdvice category data both reflect this ladder, with buyers citing reporting, consolidation, and multi-entity management as the deciding factors. When to actually migrate off QuickBooks, and how long a NetSuite cutover takes, is its own decision that we cover separately, and this software chapter sits under our broader multi-entity accounting guide. How Indinero Approaches Multi-Entity Software Selection The software is only as good as the close discipline behind it. A native multi-entity ledger automates due-to and due-from entries and rule-based eliminations, but ASC 810 consolidation still needs a CPA to define the elimination rules, validate the roll-up, and stand behind the consolidated statements at audit. A CPA still owns the sign-off. That’s the layer indinero owns, regardless of platform. Our CPA team is deliberately platform-agnostic. We work inside QuickBooks Online, Sage Intacct, and NetSuite every day, so your books stay portable and the recommendation tracks your actual entity count and audit horizon, not a referral fee. That matters at this decision point. The most expensive mistake is jumping to a full ERP a company doesn’t need. The second is staying on spreadsheet eliminations two years too long. Because bookkeeping, accounting, tax, and fractional CFO advisory sit in one engagement, the platform choice, the close, and the tax position stay aligned instead of siloed. The books come out accrual basis and audit-ready by default, defensible to your auditor from the start. With continuous operations since 2009, the team that sets up your consolidation is the team that still owns it at next year’s audit. For growth-stage SaaS and mid-market groups weighing the jump, indinero’s accounting services are built around exactly this consolidation work. Picking the platform is the easy part. Running the eliminations, month after month, is the work. If your close is starting to feel like the job, it might be time for a different approach. Frequently asked questions Common questions on multi entity accounting software, from QuickBooks Online limits to choosing between Sage Intacct and NetSuite, are answered below. Can QuickBooks Online handle multiple entities in one account? No, QuickBooks Online has no native multi-entity consolidation, so each legal entity needs its own subscription, chart of accounts, and login. Class and location tracking can segment activity inside a single file, but that’s not a substitute for separate legal-entity ledgers. For two or three domestic entities, indinero often keeps you in QuickBooks with a consolidation add-on, then moves you to a native ledger once manual eliminations start bottlenecking the close. At what point does a company outgrow QuickBooks for multi-entity work? A company outgrows QuickBooks for multi-entity work when manual eliminations become the bottleneck of the close, not at a set revenue line. That moment commonly lands around the $10M to $20M mark or when the close crosses two weeks. The second trigger is the foreign-subsidiary test. Once you translate foreign entities at daily rates and file locally in several countries, a native consolidation engine stops being optional. Indinero times that move to your entity count and audit horizon. How much does multi-entity accounting software typically cost? Multi entity accounting software typically runs from about $25 to $90 per entity monthly on Xero up to $25,000 to $100,000-plus yearly for NetSuite OneWorld. Sage Intacct sits between, quote-only, with third-party estimates putting annual spend from roughly $15,000 into six figures once consolidation and revenue-recognition modules are added. These are indicative figures, not published rates. Indinero helps you size the tier to your entity count and audit horizon so you don’t overbuy a full ERP you don’t need. Is Sage Intacct or NetSuite better for multi-entity consolidation? Neither Sage Intacct nor NetSuite is automatically better for multi-entity consolidation. Scope, not headcount, makes the call. Choose Sage Intacct when you need accounting depth and consolidation without a full ERP footprint, a common fit around $5M to $200M revenue. Choose NetSuite OneWorld when you have many foreign subsidiaries, native multi-currency across a deep hierarchy, and a single system that also runs inventory or supply chain. Indinero works in both and recommends based on your actual scope, not a referral fee. Do consolidation add-on tools replace a true multi-entity ledger? No, consolidation add-on tools produce management reports, not a true multi-entity ledger that posts eliminations as journal entries with an audit trail. Tools like Fathom can pull each QuickBooks or Xero file into a group report, but the vendors themselves say the output isn’t audit-ready consolidated statements. Netted in a report isn’t eliminated on the books. For a near-term audit, that gap matters, which is why indinero’s CPA team owns the ASC 810 eliminations and stands behind the numbers. How long does a migration to a multi-entity platform usually take? A migration to a multi-entity platform has no single timeline, because entity count, data history, foreign subsidiaries, and integrations set the pace. A two-entity domestic move onto Sage Intacct is far lighter than a deep NetSuite OneWorld hierarchy spanning many currencies and tax jurisdictions. What matters most is clean opening balances and a defined chart of accounts before cutover. Indinero runs the migration and, with continuous operations since 2009, still owns your consolidation at next year’s audit. What should a company do about consolidation while it is still between systems? While between systems, a company should keep entity-level books clean and run interim consolidation in a controlled spreadsheet with documented eliminations and an audit trail. The risk is treating netted board-deck reports as if they were eliminated on the ledger. They aren’t. Keep intercompany entries matched due-to and due-from each period so nothing inflates group results. Indinero often bridges this gap, running the close and the eliminations on your current files while planning the move to a native ledger.

title: Annexon Expands Vonaprument Phase 3 Program in Geographic Atrophy with Addition of Month 24 Dual Primary Endpoint Complementing Month 15 Primary Endpoint and Launch of Open-Label Extension Study
summary: BRISBANE, Calif., Aug. 12, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Annexon, Inc. (Nasdaq: ANNX), a biopharmaceutical company advancing the next generation platform of targeted immunotherapies for multiple neuroinflammatory diseases that impact nearly 10 million people worldwide, today announced the addition of a
body_text: PDF Version BRISBANE, Calif., Aug. 12, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Annexon, Inc. (Nasdaq: ANNX), a biopharmaceutical company advancing the next generation platform of targeted immunotherapies for multiple neuroinflammatory diseases that impact nearly 10 million people worldwide, today announced the addition of a Month 24 dual primary endpoint to complement the current Month 15 primary endpoint in its Phase 3 ARCHER II trial, and launch of an open-label extension (OLE) study of vonaprument for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) with geographic atrophy (GA). With a dual primary endpoint strategy, ARCHER II can achieve success in protecting against vision loss at either Month 15 or 24, which are independent efficacy timepoints. “Our objective is to maximize the best-in-class potential of vonaprument to preserve visual acuity for millions of patients at risk of irreversible vision loss. The strong power and execution of our Phase 3 ARCHER II trial provide a clear opportunity to seamlessly incorporate a Month 24 dual primary endpoint while maintaining the Month 15 primary endpoint,” said Douglas Love, president and chief executive officer of Annexon. “As ARCHER II was already designed to remain masked through Month 24, this strategic addition allows us to also evaluate the longer-term profile of vonaprument for inclusion into the label without change to the study operation. We look forward to delivering the Month 15 data milestone on schedule in the fourth quarter of this year and delivering Month 24 data thereafter as a separate and additional assessment.” In the ongoing global, double-masked Phase 3 ARCHER II trial, all eligible patients have received at least 12 months of treatment, with masked event accrual in line with projections. The study retains strong statistical power and continues to be well-executed with a low discontinuation rate (<10%) and high compliance (>95%), reinforcing significant enthusiasm by physicians and patients. Upon completion of Month 24, all patients have the option to receive monthly vonaprument treatment in the OLE study. The OLE study is designed to evaluate the long-term safety and benefit of vonaprument in patients with GA. An independent Data Monitoring Committee (DMC) will assess the primary endpoint of the overall study at Month 15, and the Company expects to report the DMC’s assessment in the fourth quarter of 2026. Following this assessment, the DMC may recommend that the ARCHER II overall study has met its Month 15 primary endpoint, enabling the planned analysis of the trial's two sub-studies, with results anticipated in the first quarter of 2027; or it may recommend that the study continues until the Month 24 primary endpoint analysis. Completion of ARCHER II, including the Month 24 analyses, is expected in the third quarter of 2027. Vonaprument has received FastTrack Designation from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration and is the only GA program to receive PRIME designation from the European Medicines Agency (EMA). Vonaprument was also selected by EMA for the exclusive Product Development Coordinator (PDC) pilot launched in July 2025 to assist PRIME designation holders in navigating regulatory interactions, including expedited scientific advice, Marketing Authorisation Application submission readiness activities, and ad-hoc queries throughout the development program. About Vonaprument (formerly ANX007) Vonaprument is a clinical-stage investigational antigen-binding fragment (Fab) designed as a first-in-kind therapeutic to selectively inhibit C1q, the initiating molecule of the classical complement pathway and a key driver of neurodegeneration. It is formulated for intravitreal (IVT) administration, with the potential to be the first targeted vision-preserving therapy for GA. Vonaprument involves a differentiated neuroprotective approach designed to protect photoreceptor cells and retinal function by blocking C1q and the entire classical pathway, while allowing for normal immune activity of the lectin and alternative complement pathways. Vonaprument has been granted Fast Track designation from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and is the first therapeutic candidate for the treatment of GA to receive Priority Medicine (PRIME) designation from the EMA for the treatment of GA. About the Phase 2 ARCHER Trial ARCHER is a successfully completed, randomized, multi-center, double-masked, sham-controlled Phase 2 trial that evaluated vonaprument in a broad population of patients with GA. Across multiple measures, vonaprument consistently preserved visual function and ellipsoid zone retinal structure, reinforcing the therapeutic potential of protecting photoreceptor health early in disease progression. Vonaprument provided significant, time and dose-dependent protection from vision loss as measured by confirmed best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) ≥15-letter loss, the widely accepted and clinically meaningful functional endpoint. Significant protection from vision loss was also shown in other prespecified measures of BCVA and visual function, including low luminance visual acuity (LLVA) and low luminance visual deficit (LLVD). Vonaprument was also shown to protect key retinal structures important for vision, including significant protection of photoreceptors as measured by optical coherence tomography (OCT). Vonaprument was generally well-tolerated through month 12, with no increase in choroidal neovascularization (CNV) rates between the treated and sham arms and no events of retinal vasculitis reported. About the Phase 3 ARCHER II Trial ARCHER II is an ongoing global, pivotal, Phase 3 sham-controlled, double-masked trial of vonaprument in 659 patients with GA, a disease driven by early photoreceptor degeneration leading to vision loss. Enrollment was completed in July 2025. The primary endpoints of this two-year trial are the proportion of patients with confirmed best corrected visual acuity 15-letter loss at two consecutive visits, measured through months 15 and 24. Best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) ≥15-letter loss represents three lines on the standard Early Treatment of Diabetic Retinopathy Study (ETDRS) eye chart. Proportion of patients experiencing BCVA ≥15-letter loss is a well-established functional endpoint that has served as the basis for numerous ophthalmology drug approvals by the FDA and European Medicines Agency. Secondary endpoints in ARCHER II include safety, LLVA, and photoreceptor integrity (EZ). A global registration path has been established with U.S. and European regulators for ARCHER II. ARCHER II is a single protocol that will also be analyzed as two sub-studies after meeting the primary endpoint. Topline results from the Month 15 primary analysis are expected in the fourth quarter of 2026. About Annexon Annexon Biosciences (Nasdaq: ANNX) is advancing the next generation platform of targeted immunotherapies for nearly 10 million people worldwide living with serious neuroinflammatory diseases. Our founding scientific approach focuses on C1q, the initiating molecule of a potent inflammatory pathway that when misdirected can lead to tissue damage and loss of function in a host of diseases. Our targeted therapies are designed to stop classical complement-driven neuroinflammation at its source to provide meaningful functional benefit and alter the course of disease. Annexon’s mission is to deliver game-changing therapies to patients so that they can live their best lives. To learn more visit annexonbio.com . body_text: A tragic case involving a first-time mother who died after developing a rare and life-threatening pregnancy complication has raised concerns about the importance of thorough antenatal assessments and communication between healthcare teams. Gemma Robins, a 30-year-old data analyst from Hove, died after spending 40 days in intensive care following the birth of her daughter. According to an inquest, there had been an opportunity during a late-pregnancy appointment to investigate possible signs of pre-eclampsia and other serious complications. The case has prompted renewed attention on pregnancy warning signs, antenatal care and the potentially serious condition known as acute fatty liver of pregnancy, or AFLP. What happened to Gemma Robins? Gemma had reportedly experienced severe sickness throughout her pregnancy. At her 36-week antenatal appointment in April 2024, concerns were recorded about high blood pressure and slowed growth of her baby. She also told healthcare professionals that she could not feel her baby moving. The inquest heard that her urine was not tested for possible signs of pre-eclampsia and that her blood pressure should have been checked again. The coroner concluded that this represented a missed opportunity to investigate whether she was developing a serious pregnancy-related condition. Two days later, Gemma became acutely unwell and was taken to Worthing Hospital. She was unable to keep food or fluids down and ultimately underwent an emergency caesarean section. Her baby was born in very poor condition, while Gemma's own health continued to deteriorate. Tests showed abnormalities affecting her liver and kidneys. She was later transferred to intensive care at Royal Sussex Hospital in Brighton. A rare and dangerous pregnancy condition Gemma was diagnosed with acute fatty liver of pregnancy, a rare disorder that can occur during the third trimester. AFLP can interfere with the normal functioning of the liver and may develop rapidly. If not recognised and treated promptly, it can become life-threatening for both mother and baby. The condition can cause a range of symptoms, including nausea and vomiting, abdominal pain, loss of appetite, extreme tiredness, excessive thirst and jaundice. Because some of these symptoms can overlap with ordinary pregnancy complaints, recognising a serious change in a pregnant woman's health can be challenging. That is why healthcare professionals may need to consider the overall picture, including blood pressure, urine results, blood tests and changes in symptoms. The British Liver Trust describes AFLP as a rare but serious condition that requires urgent medical attention. The importance of recognising pre-eclampsia The inquest also focused on possible pre-eclampsia. Pre-eclampsia is a pregnancy complication associated with high blood pressure and can affect organs including the liver and kidneys. Regular antenatal appointments are designed to identify warning signs and determine whether further investigation is needed. Urine testing can be used as part of an assessment for protein in the urine, while blood pressure measurements and blood tests can provide additional information about a person's condition. In Gemma's case, the coroner said blood tests might have revealed abnormal liver function and potentially resulted in an earlier hospital admission. However, the coroner also stressed that it could not be established whether earlier intervention would have prevented her death. This distinction is important. The findings identified a missed opportunity for investigation, but they did not conclude that the missed checks directly caused Gemma's death. A devastating medical deterioration After giving birth, Gemma's condition became increasingly serious. She developed severe acute necrotising pancreatitis, a particularly dangerous form of pancreatitis in which parts of the pancreas and surrounding tissue can become damaged or die. She also experienced sepsis, liver dysfunction, kidney injury and complications involving her caesarean section wound. Weeks later, Gemma suffered internal bleeding. A transfer to Royal Surrey County Hospital was delayed while specialist teams were being contacted. She eventually underwent emergency surgery but died on June 13 after doctors concluded that there was nothing further they could do. Her death was attributed to multi-organ failure, severe acute necrotising pancreatitis and acute fatty liver of pregnancy. Coroner calls for lessons to be learned West Sussex, Brighton and Hove Senior Coroner Penelope Schofield concluded that Gemma died from natural causes but identified areas where improvements could potentially protect other patients. The coroner indicated that a Prevention of Future Deaths report would be issued concerning the antenatal care Gemma received. A further report was also expected to address communication difficulties between hospitals during her treatment and transfer. Such reports are intended to highlight circumstances that could present risks to other people and encourage organisations to consider whether changes are necessary. The healthcare organisations involved have expressed condolences to Gemma's family and said they were reviewing the findings. Royal Surrey NHS Foundation Trust said communication between hospitals had presented challenges and that it was committed to improving its systems. University Hospitals Sussex also expressed sympathy to Gemma's loved ones and said it welcomed the opportunity to reflect on the coroner's findings. What pregnancy symptoms should not be ignored? Although many symptoms during pregnancy can have relatively harmless explanations, sudden or severe changes should always be taken seriously. Pregnant women should seek urgent medical advice if they experience symptoms such as severe or persistent vomiting, severe abdominal pain, significant swelling, severe headache, visual disturbances, unusual breathlessness, jaundice, heavy bleeding or noticeably reduced fetal movement. This does not mean that these symptoms always indicate a life-threatening condition. Instead, they can be warning signs that require professional assessment. Anyone who is pregnant and concerned about new or worsening symptoms should contact their maternity team, doctor or emergency healthcare service as appropriate. Why antenatal appointments matter Routine antenatal care provides opportunities to identify potential complications before they become emergencies. Blood pressure checks, urine tests, questions about symptoms and monitoring the baby's growth can all form part of pregnancy care. Depending on the circumstances, healthcare professionals may also recommend blood tests, scans or hospital assessment. Gemma's case demonstrates why changes in symptoms and clinical measurements should be considered together rather than in isolation. It also highlights the importance of patients being encouraged to speak up when something feels different or when symptoms become more severe. Healthcare communication is equally important. When a patient needs to move between hospitals or specialist teams, accurate information and timely communication can help support continuity of care. A family's heartbreaking loss Gemma's parents described their daughter as warm, caring and protective. They said she had been excited about becoming a mother and had spent months preparing for the arrival of her baby. They expressed hope that the inquest would lead to meaningful lessons, particularly for women who raise concerns during pregnancy or show potential signs of serious complications. Their loss illustrates the devastating human impact that can follow a severe pregnancy complication. While no single case can establish that a different medical decision would necessarily have changed the outcome, investigations such as inquests can identify areas where healthcare systems may be strengthened. Final thoughts The death of Gemma Robins has drawn attention to several important issues in maternity care, including recognising pregnancy warning signs, investigating abnormal findings and maintaining effective communication between healthcare providers. Acute fatty liver of pregnancy is rare, but its potentially rapid progression means that awareness of symptoms and prompt medical assessment are important. The case also underlines a broader message for expectant mothers: severe, unusual or worsening symptoms should not simply be dismissed as a normal part of pregnancy. Seeking professional advice can help determine whether further assessment is needed. For healthcare services, the case serves as a reminder of the importance of comprehensive antenatal checks and clear communication when concerns arise. Most pregnancies do not develop these rare complications, but knowing the warning signs and seeking appropriate medical advice can help ensure potentially serious problems are investigated as quickly as possible. Source The Sun published on August 13, 2026. Disclaimer This article is for general informational purposes only and is not medical advice. It does not diagnose, treat or prevent any medical condition. Pregnancy-related symptoms can have many different causes. Anyone who is pregnant and experiencing concerning, severe or worsening symptoms should seek advice from a qualified healthcare professional or their maternity service promptly. In an emergency, seek emergency medical care.

title: How RevenueCat launched a Shopify store without a product photoshoot
summary: Discover how RevenueCat built a mobile-first product photography workflow with Photoroom, saving thousands of dollars while launching 40–50 products.
body_text: RevenueCat had wanted to launch a branded merch store for years, but the logistics of photographing products across a fully remote team kept the project on hold. Inventory was spread across several countries, and the team only had limited in-person time. They used Photoroom to photograph products, create listings with AI, and publish everything to Shopify. The result was a professional storefront with 40–50 products, created in days instead of weeks, while saving thousands of dollars in photography costs. The challenge Merch store launch stalled by operational complexity Inventory spread across the US, UK, and Japan made studio photography impractical Traditional photography required shipping, coordination, and extensive editing Tight deadlines ruled out a conventional workflow What Photoroom unlocked Launched RevenueCat's first Shopify merch store with 40–50 products Built a mobile workflow from photo to live Shopify listing Created professional product images without a studio Published individual products in 2–3 minutes Saved several thousand dollars versus a professional photoshoot Established a scalable workflow for hundreds of future products From an idea that never happened to a store launched in days RevenueCat is the platform behind subscription infrastructure for thousands of mobile apps. While software is its core business, the company had long wanted to create a branded merchandise store for customers and community members. The ambition was there. The logistics weren't. As a fully remote company, merchandise was spread across employees in Japan, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Building a traditional photography setup would have meant shipping products, organizing studio photography, and coordinating multiple teams, all for a project that wasn't central to the business. Creating their Shopify store listings with Photoroom finally gave the team the opportunity to move forward. Steve Kelly, Content and Growth Marketing at RevenueCat, explains: "Photoroom just seemed like a really good, straightforward, easy-to-implement option that we could do pretty much with our phones." - Steve Kelly, RevenueCat Professional product photos without a studio Instead of hiring photographers or setting up a temporary studio, the RevenueCat team photographed around 40–50 products using their phones. From there, Photoroom removed backgrounds, created Ghost mannequin images where needed, cleaned up products , generated titles, descriptions, and image metadata with AI, and published everything directly to Shopify. The team also used AI Product Staging to create clean, consistent product imagery without building physical sets. The new process also replaced much of the team's editing work. Rather than switching between multiple tools for retouching and cleanup, RevenueCat's design lead completed almost everything inside Photoroom. Even small fixes, like removing wrinkles from folded apparel, were handled during editing. Accuracy mattered just as much as speed. Photoroom maintained product fidelity and kept products true to the original products with sharp logos and consistent colors. "Everything looked like the original photos. I wouldn't do a double take. The images on our site look fantastic. They look professional. There's no real difference, I don't think, for the average person." - Steve Kelly, RevenueCat One app instead of multiple tools Once the Shopify store was set up, creating a new product became a quick and almost entirely mobile process. "You can go from photo to product in your list of products on your Shopify store in probably two or three minutes." - Steve Kelly, RevenueCat Multiple team members worked in parallel, photographing, editing, and publishing products at the same time. Without a shared studio, expensive photography equipment, or a traditional workflow, the team could divide the catalog and move quickly. Compared with organising a professional product shoot, Steve estimates the company saved several thousand dollars while avoiding the challenge of shipping inventory across multiple countries. More importantly, the store finally launched. "We just wouldn't have gotten around to it without Photoroom," Steve says. Scaling for the future The current store represents only a fraction of RevenueCat's catalog. Hundreds of products remain to be photographed, making scalability increasingly important. Following the launch, the team identified additional Photoroom capabilities it plans to explore: AI-generated product videos , Listing score for Shopify optimization, and the Recolor tool to create instant color variants across SKUs. Although merchandise isn't RevenueCat's core business, Steve expects Photoroom to remain part of the team's process: "Photoroom offers a smoother workflow end to end than pretty much any other way you could do it." - Steve Kelly, RevenueCat

title: Dragstalgia: A Bit of America in Middle England
summary: The home of drag racing is, and always has been, the United States. But there’s a big following in Europe, particularly in England, where the sport has thrived since 1966, when the first meeting was held at Santa Pod, near Wellingborough, in the English Midlands. The site is actually an old World War II airbase […]
body_text: The home of drag racing is, and always has been, the United States. But there’s a big following in Europe, particularly in England, where the sport has thrived since 1966, when the first meeting was held at Santa Pod, near Wellingborough, in the English Midlands. The site is actually an old World War II airbase called Podington, which was opened in 1942 to accommodate the U.S. Air Force, particularly its 92nd Bombardment Group. In 1947, the base was decommissioned and remained largely inactive until the 1960s. Overshadowed by a wind turbine, Garry Hill’s Ford Popular “HoppinPoppin” races Ben Montgomery’s “The Green Pop.” Seems like a popular color! Mark Gillies In 1964 and ’65, U.S. drag racers competed at airfield circuits in the U.K., but the first permanent site opened on Easter Monday in 1966 at Podington, newly renamed as Santa Pod. The name was simple enough: “Santa” invoked the spirit of the cradle of drag racing, Southern California, and “Pod” is a contraction of Podington. Just like they did in the day, the Gasser Circus cars popped wheelies on demand. Brian Gibson’s Dodge Dart “Identity Crisis” takes on Emily Latham-Taylor’s Nova SS “Nurse Stoner.” Mark Gillies As well as hosting European drag championships for the FIA and FIM, the governing bodies of international car and bike motorsport, the track hosts events as diverse as drifting, VW fan fests, and nostalgia drag racing. Its premier event for these classic dragsters is Dragstalgia, now in its 15th year. This is a celebration of what many see as the golden era of drag racing in the 1960s and ’70s and is run in association with the National Street Rod Association, the U.K.’s premier club for hot rods, street rods, and customs. As well as 10 classes featuring 202 drag car and bike entries, the event also featured a beer festival, live music, a display of classic drag machines, a car show, and a chance for people to drive their cars in the “Run What You Brung” category. Gavin Meanley adopts period race gear in a very historic dragster, Dean Butler’s Ford flathead-powered 1963 “Charles Bang Special.” Mark Gillies Funnily enough, when we attended this three-day festival at the end of June, the weather was more like Pomona than Podington: blue skies, with temperatures in the 80s and 90s. We could have been transported far away from Merry Olde England thanks to the heady smells of burning rubber and nitro fumes on the track and meat grilling in the campsites, along with the sounds of rockabilly and roaring V-8s. The 10 classes covered the gamut, from Superstock to Top Fuel dragsters and Funny Cars. We trawled the pits, looking for dragsters you might not ordinarily see in the U.S. We stumbled across Fiat Topolino Altereds and a whole class for British Ford Anglias, Populars, and Fordsons from the 1940s and ’50s, mixed in with the kind of machinery you’d see, well, at Pomona. Here are five standouts. Austin Devon Pickup: “Glenn & Glenn” / Gasser Circus The heart of the pickup is a 472-cubic-inch Pontiac that is supercharged and fed by twin 440 Holleys. Glenn says it makes 505 hp at the wheels. Mark Gillies Originally, the pickup was going to be green, but Glenn had second thoughts when he saw so many green nostalgia dragsters. The inspiration for the orange color scheme was a local tow truck, which he tracked down to get the paint code. Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Who said old pickups are exclusively American? Simon Glenn’s Austin Devon runs in the Gasser Circus class, which invokes the heady days of the Gasser Wars of the 1960s, when blown short-wheelbase coupes and sedans fought for A, B, and C/GS honors. The Gasser Circus in the U.K. has now been going for 23 years, and the classic Tri-Chevys, Fords, and Willys from the period Gasser Wars have been joined by English Fords, Morrises, and Austins. Glenn came late to drag racing. The retired design and technology teacher first came to Santa Pod when he was 17. “I was into bikes then, racing motocross. I got into hot rods, but then I sold everything when I got married, and then had my kids. As they were getting older and didn’t need so much attention, I started building cars.” Retired teacher Simon Glenn used to race motocross but has swapped bikes for this Austin Devon pickup. Mark Gillies His first street rod was a Fiat Topolino, but he didn’t drag race that, because it had fragile Alfa Romeo running gear. Instead, he built a 1918 Buick roadster “that was made out of a shell that was a classic barn find. I even had a picture with a chicken sitting on the cowl.” The roadster was fitted with a 400-cubic-inch Pontiac V-8, so it was only natural that Glenn went with Pontiac power when he built his Gasser. The reason for going the Austin pickup route was simple: “I had a steel one, actually, many years ago,” he says. “It was mildly hot rodded, and I used it for going to work, taking stuff to the tip, just as an everyday runaround. “The inspiration for this car was the C&O Austin of Gene Ciambella, and I had a picture of it from Rod & Custom magazine on my garage wall since they invented photocopies. I thought about using the car I had, but I was having too much fun with it, and you’d lose all the value, hence the fiberglass body on this one.” Mark Gillies The car has a self-built 2×4 chassis with a 9-inch Ford rear end, a solid front end with Willys springs, and a 472-cu-in Pontiac motor with a stroker crank and a 6V71C supercharger running around 9 pounds of boost. The engine makes 505 horsepower at the wheels and drives through a TH400 reverse transmission. Glenn built the engine and fabricated a lot of pieces on the car, including gorgeous machined-from-solid linkages and shifters, as well as the wheelie bars. “You can buy wheelie bars,” he says, “but I made them. That was partly born of necessity because it’s cheaper, but also … because I can.” Mark Gillies The bright orange paint occurred by happenstance. “All along, it was going to be green,” he says. “And then I discovered, there’s a green Austin. There’s a green metallic Ford Pop. And a green Morris Z van. Coming here one day, a Ratcliffe tow truck went past me. It was a day like this, and there was a radioactive glow coming off this truck. I went to their yard, as they’re fairly local to where I live, and asked what the color was. I got the paint code, and I’m really chuffed with it. The lettering was done by Neil Melliard. He sponsors the class and has lettered quite a few of the Gasser Circus cars.” Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Glenn loves making parts for his cars: these are the manual shift levers for the TH400 transmission. Mark Gillies More Glenn artistry in metal: The beautifully machined and fabricated throttle linkage is all his own work. Mark Gillies Glenn’s had his share of mechanical issues, but the scraped paintwork on the fender was down to a family member… Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Glenn, who has run 129.8 mph at 10.145 seconds, had a trying weekend at Dragstalgia. A new radiator failed, and once that had been fixed, the car developed a fuel leak. Once he and his teenage crew had sorted that, he made the semis only to trip the timing beam. On his Facebook page, though, he’s as enthusiastic as ever: “40 days to the Mopars,” he writes. Volkswagen Beetle: “Nitro Bug” / Outlaw Nostalgia Funny Car The fuel-injected and supercharged Hemi is a thirsty beast: Raw says the Beetle goes through around eight gallons of nitro per quarter-mile run. Mark Gillies The Beetle’s engine needs a lot of maintenance: Raw says they do two runs before having the heads off to circulate the pistons. Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Andy Raw’s Beetle is a far cry from the vehicle that put large parts of the world on wheels after the end of WWII. And it’s a long way from the Beetle he started out drag racing 20 years ago, a 1200-cc Sportsman-class car. This Beetle is a fire-breathing Outlaw Nostalgia Funny Car that runs on nitro and makes more than 4000 horsepower from its 500-cubic-inch Brad Anderson Hemi. At Dragstalgia, Raw ran in the Cannonball class, with the fastest dragsters, Funny Cars, Altereds, and rails at the event. The format is unusual: The first three qualifying run times are added together and on the fourth and final run, the first and second lowest times face off for the win, with third and fourth running for third place, and so on down the order. Mark Gillies The Beetle shape was a no-brainer for Raw. “One of my businesses is old VWs, air-cooled stuff. But we take the motors out, fit Subaru engines, we do our own gearboxes, ABS, traction control, electric power steering, all of that stuff. I love Beetles. I love the shape. “I had another VW Funny Car before this. I managed to find the original mold from Brian Burrows’ Outrage dragster, which ran here. And then I went as far as I could with an alcohol blown motor. So, the decision was made to go nitro. That was my progression. I’ve never sat still.” Andy Raw runs several businesses, but he’s a die-hard VW Beetle fan, which explains the body on his nostalgia funny car. Mark Gillies Raw’s best time with the Beetle is a 5.84 on the full quarter-mile, which the nostalgia class runs. “The car was built to run sixes,” he says. “I never thought I’d ever go that fast. My 1000-foot speed was 237 mph and I kind of bottled it. I love driving the car. People love the car. When I finish competition driving, I ain’t gonna sell it. It’ll just come out at these meetings. I love my lifestyle and my lifestyle events. We’ve got Bug Jam coming next, which is the biggest VW event in Europe. Every year, we get asked to come and we just put on a show for the crowd.” Running a Funny Car, even on the nostalgia circuit, is an expensive business. The Beetle goes through about 8 gallons a run, most of which is used doing warmups. It uses less fuel on the actual run because it’s making power inside the motor rather than dumping it out the headers. The Beetle has something far more potent than a four-cylinder air-cooled motor: The Brad Anderson Hemi runs on nitro and makes more than 4000 hp. Mark Gillies Raw lists his sponsors, including American company Dunn & Gone Racing, Westwood Cylinder Liners, and main sponsor Cool Flo. “You do need sponsors. It helps massively. It really, really does. These cars are mental expensive to run. I mean, we go through a barrel of nitro, which is about 1500 quid [about $2000]. We go through a barrel of oil, which is another 1500 quid.” Mark Gillies Raw’s team doesn’t totally rebuild the engine after every run, but they do take the heads off and circulate the pistons after two runs. He says he gets 25 runs out of a crankshaft, whether the car runs the full quarter or goes 100 feet. “Everything is a consumable on these engines. One of the reasons we strip them is that if something like a bearing that costs 10 bucks fails, it can destroy a whole engine. So, you have to keep on top of it if you want to run fast and hard.” Mark Gillies It takes a lot of money to run these cars, so sponsors are important. Raw says: “If you want to run fast and hard, it costs.” Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Underneath the Beetle body, this is a classic funny car, down to monster rear Hoosier slicks. Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Raw has been bitten so heavily by the drag-racing bug that he has raced some modern Funny Cars that will clear 300 mph. He says of drag racing: “It’s a life. It’s a family thing. My kids grew up on this track. I’ve been doing this for so long. And, you know, the guys who work on the car, they do it for free, they become lifelong friends. And I’ve been doing it that long now that I can’t see myself doing anything else. My next step would be to retire, but that ain’t happening anytime soon.” Ford Anglia: “Al’s Gasser” / Outlaw Anglia The line is from Motorhead’s song, “Ace of Spades:” You win some, lose some / It’s all the same to me. Mark Gillies Under the hood, “Al’s Gasser” runs a naturally aspirated 362-cubic-inch Chevy making around 550 hp. He ran a 10.026-second pass at Dragstalgia at 129.78 mph for the quarter. Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Al O’Connor has been racing his Ford Anglia for more than 50 years and is a member of the British Drag Racing Hall of Fame. His Anglia runs in the Outlaw Anglia class, which has been around for 34 years. These classic 1940s and ’50s Ford Popular and Anglia sedans, vans, and pickups are short and squat, but are also seriously fast; the record for this class is 6.77 seconds at 203.49 mph. O’Connor was at Santa Pod from the get-go. “I lived around here and came up in 1966, when they first opened. I was here on the first day, and I was like, this is brilliant! The Americans had come over with all their big stuff and there was an Anglia with a small-block Chevy in it. I thought, I could do with one of them.” Al O’Connor has been racing his Ford Anglia for more than 50 years and is a member of the British Drag Racing Hall of Fame. Mark Gillies Mark Gillies So he did. “I started drag racing ’cause, in its day, it was cheap motorsport and anyone could do it. You could go down to a junkyard and pick up everything you wanted. Weld it together, or pop rivet it together, or do whatever you want. Everything was built out of junkyards, but nowadays, obviously, you just buy everything from America. Nowadays, you need a bit of money.” He first ran this Anglia in 1974 but crashed it and in 1978 replaced it with the car you see here. The chassis was built by Alan “Bootsie” Herridge, a legend of the U.K. drag racing scene, and O’Connor finished it off. Unlike most of the cars running at Dragstalgia, the Anglia has a steel body. “This has got a fiberglass front end,” says O’Connor, “but the rest of it is all proper Ford. I have Mustang A-arm front suspension with a 9-inch Ford rear end and a Powerglide. I’ve been through a lot of gearboxes. Started off with a Jag[uar], then went to a Muncie, then went to a Liberty. But I decided not to have a clutch and went to an automatic. It’s popular, because it’s consistent.” O’Connor hasn’t just raced his car in the U.K.—he took it to the U.S. in the late 1980s and “nearly got a win in the semis in Georgia in 1988”. Mark Gillies The engine is a naturally aspirated 362-cubic-inch Chevy with a single four-barrel Holley, running on pump gas. “It used to have 600 hp,” says O’Connor, “but it’s now down to around 550. It has run 9.50 but these days it’s in the 9.9s. I can’t win outright in my Anglia anymore. The cars have got too fast.” On the Ford’s dash, there’s an NHRA sticker from the days when O’Connor ran SuperGas in the U.S. “I ran the semis in Georgia and nearly got a win. I didn’t know about timers at the time. Still don’t…“ Connor says he has always been a mechanic, “but computers came into the world, and I ended up working on old cars. People are now tuning with laptops, but I tune with a screwdriver and pliers. I just need pliers to open up the secondaries on the butterflies on the carb when I run 9.9s. There’s nothing trick on this car. I learned about wheelie bars back in the 1970s when I tried doing it without them. Stood it on its back end so I run them now.” Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Mark Gillies O’Connor crashed the car in 2026 and, according to fellow Outlaw Anglia competitor Phil Middleton: “Al said he should cut it up after the crash. We sat in the bar chatting and I said we could repair that. His car is what got me into this.” O’Connor takes up the story: “It was rebuilt with help from everyone in the paddock. Everyone chipped in. A wheel from here, a wheel from there. Didn’t really cost a lot and worked out all right.” Ford Anglia: “Acute Angle” / Supercharged Outlaws After Dale’s recent accident, new funny car headers appeared on the Anglia. They’re attached to an injected and supercharged 355 cubic-inch small-block Chevy. Mark Gillies An AutoMeter Sport-Comp tach provides all-important information, including shift lights. Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Among the Nitro Altereds, Ford coupes, and insane muscle cars in a class of serious supercharged horsepower and quarter-mile times below 9.90, Paul Dale’s Supercharged Outlaw Ford 105E Anglia stood out. Not just because I grew up loving the shape of these cars, with their reversed rear window, but because of its proportions. It’s got a short wheelbase and it’s narrow. Dale says: “I used to go to the Chelsea Cruise years ago. There was always a dark metallic green Anglia there. And I just fell in love with it from that day and always wanted an Anglia. This body came up on eBay one day, so I thought, right, this is it. We’re doing it. Builder Paul Dale was lucky to be at Dragstalgia: he hit the wall at his previous meeting and had to “do a hell of a lot of bodywork” to get the car ready in time Mark Gillies “Me and my dad built it about 11 years ago. We put a bog-standard Chevy engine in it and just came racing for a bit of fun. Back then, we were running 11s, and we got into the 10s. As soon as I got into the 10s, I wanted a nine. When we got into the nines, I wanted an eight. And then last year, we broke the world record for a Ford 105E Anglia, a 7.71 at 174 mph. Mark Gillies “A very good friend of mine, Andy Robinson, builds drag cars for a living, and he actually told me I was crazy. Even after driving the car for 10 years, I still get in it, and I’m shaking like a leaf. You’ve only got to lose traction slightly on one wheel and the car just steers itself.” He found that out weeks before Dragstalgia when the car hooked right into the wall at around 150 mph and they had to race to rebuild it in time for this event. The Anglia has a steel body over a full tube CDS ( cold-drawn seamless ) chassis. Dale says the wheelbase was stretched to 100 inches to give a bit more stability. It runs a 355 small-block Chevy with a Motown block and Dart Iron Eagle heads, an 871 blower, hat injection, and methanol. Dale says it makes around 1100 horsepower and that while running methanol was difficult at first, it has made a huge difference to a car that was always overheating. Mark Gillies He uses a two-speed Powerglide transmission. The back axle is—yep, you guessed it—a 9-inch Ford, with Capri struts up front and Mark 2 Escort brakes. ”Luckily,” he says, “we get a mile to stop. It’s not a very technical car, if I’m honest. It’s got an Enderle mechanical fuel pump on it, so, you know, there’s nothing high tech. It’s well old school.” Dale got into drag racing through his father, who raced a Fiat Topolino Altered. “When I started getting the buzz for it, he said, ‘right, you can start driving.’ I carried on for about five or six years, I suppose, and then I got into girls and lost interest in drag racing.” Mark Gillies He’s back into it now, though. “The main reason for me coming back is I’m at an age where my mum and dad are still around and they adore drag racing. I’ve got a disabled daughter who’s 24, who absolutely loves drag racing. My wife Emma loves drag racing. So it’s really an excuse to get us all out and spend the weekend together. And honestly, having my dad here at 80, still crewing for me, and still coming down on that start line every run, it’s just amazing. Yes, the toy dog atop the parachute goes all the way down the strip with the Anglia, even when Dale was running 157.96 mph and 8.617 seconds in qualifying. Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Mark Gillies In his day job, Dale runs a building company. “I’m always stressed,” he says. “As soon as I get through the gates here, it’s like a release. Just switch off, concentrate on the car, and spend time with family and friends. That’s what I love about it. Yeah, it’s an amazing hobby.” Plymouth Superbird: “43” / Nostalgia Superstock Hood-mounted gauges weren’t standard on a Superbird but are useful on a dragstrip when you’re going 130 mph in the quarter. Mark Gillies The famous Road Runner logo adorns the rear wing of this Superbird, which features a paint scheme that pays homage to “The King,” Richard Petty. Mark Gillies Mark Gillies In among a sea of Superstock Chevy Novas and Camaros, Plymouth Barracudas and Dodge Challengers, I spotted Don Scott’s Plymouth Superbird. Its wild rear wing and prow of a nose make it look special enough, but it also has the distinctive color scheme of NASCAR great Richard “The King” Petty. “I’ve just been fascinated by Petty, always thought he was a great racer,” says Scott. “And I always loved the look of his car, and the fact the Superbird walked him back from Fords when he was racing Torinos in 1969.” Don Scott is unusual in that he has not only drag raced his Superbird, but gone circuit racing with it as well. Mark Gillies Scott says he used to own a genuine Superbird. “Six-pack, four-speed, but it was too valuable to do anything with. I wanted to race one, so I bought this kit in South Carolina 20 years ago and converted it into this lookalike Superbird.” Under the wild bodywork, there’s a naturally aspirated 572-cubic-inch all-aluminum Keith Black Hemi with twin Holley 1050 Dominators. The monster Keith Black Hemi underhood is naturally aspirated, runs twin Holley 1050 Dominators, and makes 860 hp on the dyno. Mark Gillies Scott says that it has been dyno’d at 860 horsepower and should go “about 9.4/9.5 at 150.” The engine drives through a race-built TorqueFlite transmission to a 9-inch Ford rear end that “is unbreakable and gave me options to run different ratios for the drag strip or the race track. If you run a Dana rear end, you have to strip it to change ratios.” Scott says the rules for Superstock in the U.K. aren’t the same as they are in the U.S. “I used to be on the committee. A lot of them I invented myself, just things that are unique to appeal to the limited number of cars we’ve got in the country.” Mark Gillies “In the States, they’ve got thousands of them,” he continues. “The best we can put together, I think, is we’ve had 72 cars here. And that’s pretty much it. There’s not much else that’s race orientated among American muscle in this country. We’ve got to have stock suspension, which is totally different to the rules in the States. We have different tire regulations—we can run 10.5-inch-wide tires on a 10-inch rim. We haven’t got any limitations on back axles.” Before he retired, Scott split his time between the U.K., Canada, and the U.S. “So I kind of grew up with drag racing. I’ve raced in other classes, like Pro ET, but I could be racing a Morris Minor as long as it went quicker than 11.99. But I like mixing it with muscle cars, and this is the class for the Superbird, really.” Mark Gillies Unusually for a drag car, Scott’s Superbird has been used on the circuits as well, running against old NASCAR stock cars. “I got into a proper scrap with an ex-Jeff Gordon #24 stock car at Brands Hatch once,” Scott says. “And I was actually quicker down the straights, but they’re like on rails in the corners and I was hanging on for dear life. I’d have them dead on the straights, and they’d have me on the corners, and it kind of panned out fairly equal in the end. And the crowd loved my sideways antics around corners, particularly around Druids.” Scott won the Nostalgia Superstock title in 2022 after deciding to concentrate on the drag strips. “They both have their own appeals in different ways. In the U.K., we were limited to racing in Bernie Codosh’s V-8 series , but the thing against that was that you had to sign up and do a certain amount of the series. Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Mark Gillies “The beauty in this sport—and it’s because we’ve got a big family as well—I can take it or leave it, I can come and go. If I’m in the championship, you know, we’ll try and see it through. But if I don’t, it’s not the end of the world. So, I just opted for the drag scene instead of circuits.” *** Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Mark Gillies Mark Gillies The post Dragstalgia: A Bit of America in Middle England appeared first on Hagerty Media .

title: 2027 Nissan Kicks Pricing, Specs, and Release Date
summary: The Nissan Kicks was completely redesigned in 2025 with a more upright design, added tech, and available all-wheel drive. For 2027, the off-road-oriented Rock Creek trim joins the lineup.
body_text: The Nissan Kicks was completely redesigned in 2025 with a more upright design, added tech, and available all-wheel drive. It sits in the competitive subcompact crossover class and squares off against the Chevrolet Trax, Hyundai Kona, Honda HR-V, Kia Seltos, and Toyota Corolla Cross. The 2027 Nissan Kicks will have four trims: S, SV, SR, and Rock Creek. 2027 Nissan Kicks Pricing, Specs, and Release Date What’s New for the 2027 Nissan Kicks Design Powertrain Interior Technology Safety Pricing and Release Date Further Research What’s New for the 2027 Nissan Kicks Since the Nissan Kicks was all-new in 2025, it doesn’t receive any big sweeping changes across the lineup for this model year. However, what Nissan does do for 2027 is add the Rock Creek trim to the Kicks lineup. Built off of the SV trim, the Rock Creek adds more features and technology designed for off-road driving. The new Kicks Rock Creek will come standard with all-wheel drive, an exclusive Off-Road driving mode, and hill descent control as well as some unique design treatments. Design The 2027 Nissan Kicks has an upright stance with sharp edges and a unique vertical stack front lighting signature that echoes the one found on the Nissan Murano. The base S trim comes with 16-inch steel wheels, but 17- and 19-inch wheels are available as you level up in trims. The Rock Creek model is differentiated by exclusive 17-inch black alloy wheels, gloss black exterior accents, a roof rack with cross bars that can hold up to 165 pounds, and amber daytime running lights. Powertrain The Nissan Kicks is equipped with a 141-horsepower, 2.0-liter, four-cylinder engine paired with a continuously variable transmission. Front-wheel drive is standard, and all-wheel drive is available on all trims. EPA estimates that the FWD models will get 28 mpg in the city and 35 mpg on the highway, with AWD models getting 27 mpg and 34 mpg, respectively. All trims of the Kicks have 8.4 inches of ground clearance, but the new Rock Creek adds an Off-Road mode with unique traction tuning and hill descent control to aid drivers in mild off-road situations. Interior The interior of the Nissan Kicks is a mix of modern and traditional with a large infotainment screen combined with physical-touch buttons and dials for HVAC and audio controls. Technically, the Kicks is a five-passenger vehicle, but four passengers will be more comfortable in this subcompact crossover. Cloth seats are standard with leatherette seating surfaces available in the top SR trim. The Rock Creek adds TailorFit (synthetic leather) seats and steering wheel as well as Rock Creek-branded floor mats. Though a moonroof isn’t standard on any trim, it is available in both the SV and SR premium packages. For a vehicle on the small side of the spectrum, it’s worth noting that the Kicks has a decent cargo area with up to 29.2 cubic feet of space behind the second row and up to 58.5 cubic feet behind the first row in the FWD models. AWD cargo space drops slightly to 23.9 and 50.1 cubic feet, respectively. Technology One of the surprising things about the 2027 Kicks is the amount of technology you’ll find on this affordability-focused crossover. Standard features include a 12.3-inch infotainment screen, a four-speaker audio system, two front USB-C ports, Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, and a standard 7-inch digital color display. Available features include a wireless phone charger, wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, two USB-C rear ports, heated front seats, heated steering wheel, a Wi-Fi hotspot, NissanConnect services, a myQ Connected Garage Door opener, a 10-speaker Bose sound system, and a 12.3-inch digital cluster. Search for Nissan Kicks See all 2024 Nissan Kicks $11,500 103,964 miles Includes dealer fees Great Deal Indianapolis, IN 2026 Nissan Kicks $22,399 13,419 miles Includes dealer fees Good Deal Bonita Springs, FL 2021 Nissan Kicks $10,798 106,963 miles Includes dealer fees Good Deal Jacksonville, FL 2023 Nissan Kicks $16,785 46,063 miles Includes dealer fees Great Deal Homestead, FL 2019 Nissan Kicks $11,801 63,793 miles No additional dealer fees Good Deal Draper, UT 2024 Nissan Kicks $18,171 42,022 miles Includes dealer fees Good Deal Lakewood, CO Safety Standard safety features on the 2027 Nissan Kicks include automatic emergency braking with pedestrian detection, lane departure warning, blind spot monitoring, rear cross-traffic alert, adaptive cruise control, and automatic high beams. Available safety features include automatic reverse braking, front and rear parking sensors, lane departure prevention, emergency lane keep assist, blind-spot intervention, traffic sign recognition, ProPILOT assist, and a 360-degree camera system. At the time of this writing, the 2027 Kicks had not yet been crash tested by either the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration or the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety. However, the 2026 model received an overall safety rating of four out of five stars from the NHTSA, and it gets mixed Good and Marginal crash-test scores from IIHS. Pricing and Release Date The 2027 Nissan Kicks will go on sale later this summer. At the time of this writing, Nissan lists the starting price for the S trim at $24,335. The SV and SR will start at $26,035 and $28,535, respectively. The AWD versions of these three trims start at $25,835, $28,035, and $30,335. The Rock Creek with standard AWD starts at $30,385. Outside of the SV Premium ($950) and SR Premium ($1,600) packages, the Kicks has some premium paint as well as two-tone paint options that range in price from $450 to $1,000. Plus, a cold weather package available on SV and SR trims ($300) adds heated front seats, heated steering wheel, heated side mirrors, and rear floor heater ducts. title: The Bitcoin Fork That Lasted Two Blocks
summary: The soft fork that was supposed to save Bitcoin from “spam" lasted two blocks.
body_text: This article originally appeared in Galaxy Research's weekly newsletter. Subscribe to get timely insights delivered to your inbox every Friday morning. The soft fork that was supposed to save Bitcoin from “spam" lasted two blocks . BIP-110, formally the Reduced Data Temporary Softfork, was the brainchild of pseudonymous developer Dathon Ohm with input from Luke Dashjr, creator of the Bitcoin Knots node software, former chairman and CTO of the Ocean mining pool, and a polarizing figure in the Bitcoin community. It called for a one-year consensus-level restriction on arbitrary data in Bitcoin transactions. This includes Ordinals inscriptions (Bitcoin’s answer to NFTs), BRC-20 and Runes (both fungible token standards), and oversized OP_RETURN . The proposal contained seven rules capping most outputs at 34 bytes, OP_RETURN at 83, data pushes at 256, plus restrictions on Taproot annexes and control blocks. The activation design targeted 55% miner signaling (1,109 of 2,016 blocks). By comparison, Bitcoin’s SegWit upgrade in 2017 wanted 95% and Taproot in 2021 wanted 90%. If 55% wasn’t reached, a mandatory signaling window opened at block 961,632, where enforcing nodes would reject any block that didn’t signal, regardless of hashrate. Miners never came close. In the last difficulty period before the window opened, 51 of 2,016 blocks signaled. That is 2.53% against a threshold its own authors had already cut nearly in half from the standard. According to block data , every one of those 51 blocks came from Ocean. Block 961,632 landed on Aug. 8 at 19:35:55 UTC. AntPool mined a non-signaling block that the network accepted, and BIP-110 nodes rejected it. Roughnecks , mining through Ocean’s DATUM system, produced the competing block. The minority chain reached 961,633 and stopped. Roughnecks quit the next day and told other miners to do the same, then reversed on Aug. 10 and resumed, saying it would keep going until a “sensible POW change” arrived. The main Bitcoin chain is now several hundred blocks ahead. Strategy Executive Chairman Michael Saylor commented on the pitiful fork attempt, saying “Bitcoin worked exactly as designed” (by remaining unaffected in the face of the ill-fated fork attempt). Ocean was the only pool signaling in favor of BIP-110. Days after the split, it disclosed that a Stratum configuration error had routed some of its miners onto the BIP-110 chain (rather than the real Bitcoin chain) for roughly 18 hours. The pool restored its default endpoint and committed to roughly 0.3 BTC in direct rebates within 72 hours. Cryptographer and Bitcoin OG Adam Back suggested the losses come out of Dashjr’s salary. Ocean’s reported hashrate has since fallen 96%, and miners have publicly called for leadership changes. On Aug. 9, Bitcoin Improvement Proposal editor Mark “Murch” Erhardt filed a motion to the Bitcoin development mailing list recommending that fellow editor Luke Dashjr be removed as an editor. Erhardt cited Dashjr’s conflict of interest, minimal contribution, championing a contentious fork, and a coordination breakdown with the other editors. The next day, it was done. Jon Atack merged the pull request (a one-line deletion) and longtime Bitcoin Core contributor Bryan Bishop confirmed the repository permissions were revoked. Bishop, Atack, Erhardt, Olaoluwa Osuntokun, and Ruben Somsen remain as BIP editors. Dashjr also announced a sabbatical from Ocean. He continues to refer to the majority chain as “Bpedo.” (One of his arguments for limiting arbitrary data was the alleged risk of child sexual abuse material being published onchain.) Dathon Ohm’s response to the 2.53% tally was to accuse the large pools of collusion and announce work on a proof-of-work change to “fire the miners.” Dashjr backed it, citing ASICBoost when pressed on what was wrong with SHA-256d, the hash function at the core of Bitcoin. (ASICBoost is a technique for speeding up mining.) OUR TAKE Ocean’s entire pitch was miner sovereignty. DATUM exists so operators build their own block templates locally instead of trusting pool operators’ block construction. That is a useful product solving a real centralization problem. Then a config error pointed unassigned hashrate at the chairman's fork for 18 hours without operator consent, and the pool ended up writing rebate checks. A movement that spent two years arguing pools are dangerous intermediaries proved its thesis at its own expense. The soft fork itself was never a “neutral anti-spam patch” as its proponents claimed. It was a consensus-level attempt to invalidate fee-paying transactions a minority of the Bitcoin community disliked. On top of that, the threshold for acceptance was cut from 95% to 55% and a mandatory window was designed to split the network if even that low bar wasn’t cleared. Lowering the threshold manufactured a quixotic attempt at a chain that needs ( by Saylor’s math ) 25 years to reach its first difficulty adjustment. BIP 148 (whose activation in 2017 is celebrated as Bitcoin Independence Day) worked because exchanges, wallets, businesses, and holders were already behind it. Miners capitulated to an economic majority that had moved without them. A UASF (user-activated soft fork) is a mechanism for the economic majority to route around miners. It is not a mechanism for ~2.5% to route around everyone. The PoW pivot makes this all worse for Ocean. Miners rejected BIP-110, and the response was to try to change the electorate. And ASIC resistance may not even be the point. Per one of the Knots strategy channels , the stated logic was to adopt an altcoin’s algorithm so ASICs would exist for the new chain on day one. Basically, cannibalize the hardware of an asset Bitcoiners would call valueless (they use an indelicate term for these; it rhymes with “bitcoin”). Bitcoin Gold ran this experiment in 2017 and nobody bothers citing it as a cautionary tale anymore. Luke Dashjr laying out proof-of-work design criteria in the Bitcoin Knots Discord channel. Source: Bitcoin.com News What to watch is whether Ocean’s 96% drawdown proves permanent. The pool building the most credible answer to Bitcoin mining centralization bet itself on a fork its chairman championed, and lost. body_text: Figure Technology Solutions Reports Strong Second Quarter 2026 Results August 13, 2026 PDF Version NEW YORK, Aug. 13, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Figure Technology Solutions (Nasdaq: FIGR; OPEN: FGRS), the leading blockchain-native capital marketplace for the origination, funding, sale and trading of tokenized assets, today announced financial results for the three and six months ended June 30, 2026. “We delivered our strongest quarter yet, headlined by 132% year-over-year volume growth in our Consumer Loan Marketplace, the addition of over 100 origination partners, and the scaling of our capital-light marketplace, with 65% of our volumes now on Figure Connect. With weekly applications now surpassing $1 billion as of July and the pending completion of our Kiavi acquisition, which we expect will significantly grow our platform into adjacent asset classes, we are accelerating our growth flywheel and our first-mover advantage in bringing the capital markets on-chain.” - Michael Tannenbaum, CEO Q2 2026 Quarterly Financial Highlights Consumer Loan Marketplace volume was $4.3 billion in the quarter, a 132% increase from the prior year.
